_note: EPPP question-type profiles, taken from Table 5 of the Orientation chapter (see text/Orientation.md). The EPPP has exactly two cognitive levels — recall and application — not a Bloom ladder. Each chapter's profile is fixed by its content domain; do not choose a profile by taste. Percentages are targets for a 50-question set, +/- 5 percentage points.

application-primary.label: Primarily application
application-primary.guidance: Most stems are hypothetical situations that require applying a standard, criterion, or rule to reach a judgment. Name the practitioner (Dr. Kennedy, a psychologist) and give a concrete situation with enough specifics to decide, then ask what they should do, whether they acted properly, or what the situation is. The remaining recall items define a term or name a specific provision. A student who memorized definitions but cannot apply them should fail most of this set.

recall-primary.label: Primarily recall
recall-primary.guidance: Most stems are short — a sentence or fragment — asking for a definition, the basic assumptions of a technique or theory, or the result of research. The application minority asks the student to identify an example of a strategy in use, or to place a hypothetical client at a stage. Distractors are sibling terms from the same framework, not invented jargon.

recall-nearly-all.label: Nearly all recall
recall-nearly-all.guidance: Short stems asking for definitions, the assumptions or predictions of a theory, research results, the function of a structure or the effect of a drug, or the purpose of a test. Only an occasional application item — typically attributing symptoms in a hypothetical case to the responsible structure, drug, or mechanism.

half-and-half.label: Half recall, half application
half-and-half.guidance: Half the items define a term. The other half give a research or testing scenario and ask which design, statistical technique, or method of evaluating reliability/validity applies — or require a short calculation such as a confidence interval. For calculation items every distractor must be the result of one specific plausible error, and whyWrong must name that error.
